analysis.answer: Current law punishes assault with up to one year in jail. The measure specifically increases the penalty for assaulting an on-duty law enforcement officer to a felony punishable by up to three years in prison.

It will likely increase direct state costs for prison operations, as individuals convicted under this statute could be incarcerated in state prisons for up to three years instead of serving shorter terms in local jails.

State taxpayers will bear the cost of longer prison sentences. Law enforcement officers may benefit from increased deterrence or incapacitation of offenders. Individuals convicted of the offense will face longer sentences and the collateral consequences of a felony record.
Prosecutors may use the threat of a felony charge and a three-year prison sentence as leverage in plea bargaining to secure convictions more efficiently.
Prosecutors gain significant discretion and negotiating power in plea deals due to the higher maximum penalty.

The deterrent effect of increasing maximum sentences is disputed. Some researchers find that longer sentences reduce crime through incapacitation and deterrence, while others argue that certainty of apprehension deters more effectively than sentence length and that longer sentences can increase recidivism.
